1.pericope_label: Him that is weak in the faith receive ye
debates: What the weakness is: Gill distinguishes weakness in the grace of faith, the trembling and misgiving sight of Christ, from weakness in the doctrine of faith, and takes the second, while Chrysostom, Theodoret, Clarke and Barnes treat it throughout as the scruple of the Jewish convert about the ceremonial law

What grounded the abstinence from flesh: Calvin rejects the heathen abstinence founded on the transmigration of souls and grounds it in fear of contamination among the heathen, Barnes and Clarke in the uncertainty whether market meat had been offered to an idol or properly bled, and Theodoret in a deliberate pretext of temperance meant to shame the Gentile converts
outliers: Calvin's report that Haldane found fault with the whole Jew and Gentile classification as unwarranted by the chapter, and his answer, with Chalmers, that the Gentiles were more probably the despisers, since Jews who had got over their prejudices would sympathise with brethren still held by them
Calvin's textual complaint that Erasmus mutilated the sentence by introducing one indeed believes in place of the repeated relative
Chrysostom's reconstruction that the abstinence from all flesh was a disguise, adopted so that abstaining from swine's flesh alone would not betray them
Robertson's report that Denney felt certain the apostle had in mind a party of vegetarians at Rome
Ellicott's aside that human nature alters very little

4.pericope_label: To his own master he standeth or falleth
debates: Whether the day-keeping itself was approved: Gill and Clarke read the sixth verse as accepting the observance because it is rendered to the Lord, while Calvin insists the notion was superstitious and that what God approved was only the refusal to act against a doubtful conscience

The perpetuity of the Sabbath: Clarke protests that the interpolated word alike makes the text abolish every distinction of days, the Sabbath included, which he holds of lasting obligation from its institution and its typical reference, while Ellicott concludes from Galatians and Colossians that the observance of days has no absolute sanction but is a question of religious expediency, and Robertson simply records that Jewish Christians kept the seventh day and Gentiles the first

The disputed clause on not regarding the day: Gill reports it absent from the Alexandrian copy and the Vulgate and Ethiopic but present in most Greek copies and in the Syriac and Arabic, while Ellicott gives it up on the authority of the best manuscripts and Robertson calls the Received Text reading not genuine
outliers: Ellicott's aside that experience seems in favour of some such system of observed days as that adopted by our own Church

Theodoret's report that the same forbearance still remained in the churches of his own day, one man embracing abstinence and another taking all kinds of food, neither condemning the other but glorying in the law of concord

Theodoret's limit on the rule, that the apostle allows this liberty of private persuasion concerning foods only, and not concerning doctrine, where he pronounces an anathema on any who preach another gospel
Calvin's distinction that the man must be left to the judgment of God while his deeds may still be judged decisively, provided the judgment is drawn from the word of God

7.pericope_label: None of us liveth to himself, and we shall all stand before the judgment seat
debates: The text of the ninth verse: Gill lists the witnesses without deciding, while Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all abandon the longer reading and rose, and revived for the shorter died and lived, Barnes judging it brought in from the margin, Clarke citing the omission by Griesbach and the verdict of Professor White that the shorter reading is indisputably genuine, and Ellicott calling the Received text a gloss upon it

Whose judgment seat is meant in the tenth verse: Ellicott states flatly that the true reading is of God, against the Received text followed by Barnes, Clarke, Calvin and Theodoret, on which the whole argument that the Father has conferred the office of judging upon Christ is built
outliers: Clarke's quotation of Heylin, that the superstitious are prone to judge and those who are not superstitious are prone to despise
Clarke's note that the Greek writers used the phrase of living to oneself for acting according to one's own judgment and following one's own opinion
Barnes's inference from the clause about dying unto the Lord that the soul is not annihilated at death but continues to belong to Christ

Calvin's turn from the doctrine to patience, that since God claims authority over our life and our death each is to bear his own condition as a yoke laid upon him and be patient under all troubles and losses
Cyril of Jerusalem's warning, drawn from the parable of the virgins, not to be confident merely in possessing the lamp but to keep it constantly burning
themes: living and dying unto the Lord
the lordship of Christ over dead and living

11.pericope_label: Every knee shall bow, and there is nothing unclean of itself
debates: What the quotation from Isaiah is for: Barnes, Wesley and Theodoret take the transfer of an oracle spoken by Jehovah to the judgment seat of Christ as proof of his divinity, Barnes saying the quotation could have been made on no other principle, while Calvin denies that it is offered as proof of anything, the judgment seat being undoubted among Christians, and holds it cited only to teach the lowliness with which that judgment is to be awaited

What by the Lord Jesus means in the fourteenth verse: Clarke and Wesley take it of an inspiration or particular revelation given to the apostle, Ellicott and Robertson read the preposition as in rather than by, a solemn asseveration out of Christian consciousness rather than a rational conclusion, and Theodoret takes it as producing the Lord of Moses against any who would ask who Paul was to legislate against Moses

Whether the verb in the eleventh verse is confess or praise: Ellicott reports that most commentators prefer praise but is not persuaded the English version is wrong, while Robertson takes the dative construction as giving praise
outliers: Gill's note that Justin Martyr cites a passage like this one as out of Ezekiel, though no such words appear there either in the Hebrew text or in the Septuagint version

Wesley's prayer at the judgment seat, that mercy in that day may be granted also to those who have differed from us, and even to those who have censured and condemned us for things done from a desire to please God or left undone from fear of offending him
Calvin's claim that the complete fulfilment of the prophecy is not now taking place, has never taken place, and is not to be hoped for in future ages, since God rules in the world only by his gospel

Calvin's distinction between the two Greek words, the first an obstacle that occasions stumbling or falling and the second one that stops progress in the way, against Wesley's quite different distinction, that the first moves a brother to act against his conscience and the second moves him to hate or judge you

Clarke's warning that it is dangerous to trifle with conscience even when it is erroneous, since a man who acts against it in one case may set aside the plainest declarations of the word of God in another

15.pericope_label: Destroy not him with thy meat; the kingdom of God is not meat and drink
debates: Whether one for whom Christ died may actually perish: Clarke draws the conclusion expressly from the emphatic Greek and Wesley states it flatly, while Calvin rejects it as contrary to many positive declarations of Scripture and holds that the apostle exhibits the tendency of such conduct without asserting that it takes effect; Calvin also refuses the softer evasion that only comfort and edification are meant, since the apostle no doubt meant the ruin of the soul

What the good is that must not be evil spoken of: Gill offers the gospel at large or the doctrine of Christian liberty, Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley take it of the liberty itself, and Theodoret takes it of faith

What righteousness and peace mean in the seventeenth verse: Ellicott denies that imputed righteousness and reconciliation with God are in view and takes them of the moral condition of the Christian and his concord with his fellow-men, while Clarke expounds righteousness as pardon of sin together with holiness of heart and life
outliers: Ellicott's textual note that the true reading opens the verse with for rather than but, and his account of a connection that leaps over the parenthesis on uncleanness to rejoin the warning against stumblingblocks

Ellicott's observation that heathen and Christian philosophers alike, Marcus Aurelius among them, have reached the conception of righteousness and peaceableness as duties, and that the peculiarity of Christianity lies in the unity it gives these attributes
Ellicott's remark on how far the description of the kingdom here converges with the sayings of the Gospels despite the wide difference of terminology between them

Clarke's caution that many so manage their good acts as to do little good and a great deal of evil by them, and that it requires much prudence and watchfulness to find the proper time of performing even a good action
Gill's note that the Vulgate and the Syriac read our good in place of your good

18.pericope_label: Follow after the things which make for peace; for meat destroy not the work of God
debates: Who the men are that approve: Barnes grants the wicked world will not love such a life but holds it will commend itself to them as the life men ought to lead, Wesley restricts the word to wise and good men, and Calvin restricts it to honest judgment, granting that the ungodly often defame the innocent and put a malignant construction on things rightly done

What the work of God is that meat destroys: Gill offers the righteousness and peace and joy just named, or the weak brother as creature and new creature, or the peace of the church, Barnes and Ellicott take it of the fabric God is rearing whether in the church or in the character, Robertson takes it of the brother for whom Christ died, and Theodoret takes it of faith itself on the authority of the saying in John that the work of God is to believe on him whom he has sent

Whether the last two clauses of the twenty-first verse belong to the text: Ellicott reports the authorities remarkably divided and decides on internal evidence to omit them as a gloss, while Calvin builds his ascending scale of weakening, stumbling and falling on all three words and Wesley expounds each of them separately
outliers: Barnes's excursus on temperance, that the caution shows what should be done now about wine, since many friends of temperance grieve at its use, and since the wine now common is mingled with alcohol and other ingredients while that of the ancients was the pure juice of the grape

Wesley's aside that practical divinity tends equally to peace and to edification while controversial divinity less directly tends to edification, though sometimes, like the builders of old, we cannot build without it
Robertson's suggestion that the warning about meat carries a side-glance at Esau and his mess of pottage
Clarke's etymology of the word for offence, originally the piece of wood or key in a trap which, being trodden on, caused the animal to fall into the pit
Calvin's revision of his own earlier distinction between the two Greek words, the idea of stumbling being given here to the word he had before explained as an impediment

22.pericope_label: Hast thou faith? Whatsoever is not of faith is sin
debates: How far the closing maxim reaches: Clarke extends it to every work done before the grace of Christ and cites the thirteenth article of his own Church that such works have the nature of sin, while Ellicott denies the extension and states that Augustine argued wrongly from this passage that the good actions of unbelievers are of the nature of sin, and Barnes grants the wider proposition to be true but denies that it is what is taught here

Whether the participle means doubting or discerning: Barnes prefers the margin, he that discerneth and putteth a difference between meats, and Theodoret reads he that maketh a distinction, while the English version has he that doubteth, which Robertson defends as hesitation and Calvin as a mind held suspended by uncertainty

Whether the opening clause is a question: Ellicott gives up the Received interrogative in deference to the four best manuscripts and reads the faith which thou hast, have to thyself, Robertson reports the same relative in the old copies, and Clarke passes on the proposal of Dr. Taylor that there is no necessity for an interrogative and that the repeated verb means thou hast a right persuasion, now hold it fast
outliers: Barnes's caution that the word rendered damned means properly to condemn, so that the verse affirms guilt and blameworthiness but not that the man will inevitably sink to hell, the same construction being required in the Corinthian warning about eating unworthily

Robertson's report that some manuscripts place the doxology at the end of this chapter rather than at the end of the epistle, which has led some to suppose the letter originally ended here and others to posit two editions of it, both of which he calls pure speculation

Calvin's protest against those who make the verse excuse devotion to foolish and superstitious ceremonies so long as the conscience is pure, since ceremonies belong to worship and are part of confession, and they who tear faith from confession take from the sun its own heat

Gill's insistence that the faith here meant is not faith in Christ and the doctrines of the gospel, which no man ought to keep in his own breast but should declare before the church and confess with the mouth
Robertson's quotation of Denney, that it is a rare felicity to have a conscience untroubled by scruples
themes: whatsoever is not of faith is sin
